title: Name Tags for a Billion Things

post.author: u/night_book_philomena
post.title: I keep the night book at the city mortuary. Last night our new cold-room printer made nine tags, and our records database says every number on them already belongs to someone buried a century ago.

blocks.text: I keep the night book at the city mortuary on Marrowgate. Every arrival gets a line in the book and a paper tag with a number, and the number goes into the Casebook, our records database, which refuses any number it already holds. Until July the numbers came from a counter at the town hall, one 25 ms trip per number. On Friday 3 July the town hall's database was down for four hours, and our printer printed nothing.

So Ingeborg, our records technician, built her own, copied from Twitter's old Snowflake. Every machine makes its own 64-bit numbers: 41 bits for the milliseconds since midnight on 1 January 2026 by the machine's own clock, 10 bits for its machine number, and 12 bits for a count within the millisecond. The desk printer is machine 1. The scanning station in the basement is machine 7. Every night from 22:00 to 06:00 it loads the city's old registers into the Casebook, one line every millisecond, each line with its own number.

On Thursday Ingeborg added a printer at the cold-room door for the night shift. She built it from a copy of the scanning station's disk, because that already had the printer software on it. Last night it made nine tags, and the Casebook refused all nine. The scanner was loading the burial registers of the old Marrowgate cemetery.
Every number was already taken, by someone buried a century ago.

22 Oct 22:00:00.000  scanner (machine 7)  started: old registers, 1 line a ms
22 Oct 22:17:41.302  cold-room printer    tag 106878672786452480
                     Casebook             REFUSED: number already in use
                     row already there    loaded 22:17:41.302 by the scanner
                                          Marrowgate burials, 1903, line 4
22 Oct 22:48:12.519  desk printer         tag 106886353467215872  saved
22 Oct 23:41:07.214  cold-room printer    tag 106899669103177728  REFUSED
   ... 6 more cold-room tags, all REFUSED; 5 more desk tags, all saved
23 Oct 05:09:28.380  cold-room printer    tag 106982301782536192  REFUSED
23 Oct 06:00:00.000  scanner (machine 7)  stopped: 28,800,000 lines

The desk printer made six tags last night, and the Casebook took every one. Ingeborg says two machines can't make the same number, because each one counts from its own clock and nothing else uses her epoch. She wants it fixed before tonight's shift. What should she change?

blocks.label: casebook_night_22oct.png

diagram.aria: Ingeborg's drawing of Thursday night, 22 October. The town hall counter, not used since July. Three machines make their own numbers and send them to the Casebook, which has a unique key on numbers. The desk printer, machine 1, made 6 tags and none were refused. The cold-room printer, built from a copy of the scanning station's disk, is machine 7 and made 9 tags; all 9 were refused. The scanning station, also machine 7, loaded 28,800,000 lines from 22:00 to 06:00, one a millisecond. Each number is 41 bits of milliseconds since 1 January 2026, a 10-bit machine number and a 12-bit count.

notes.text: Each number: 41 bits of ms since 1 Jan 2026, a 10-bit machine number, a 12-bit count

blocks.caption: Ingeborg's drawing of Thursday night. Nobody asks the town hall counter any more: each machine makes its own numbers and sends them to the Casebook, which refuses any number it already holds. The desk printer is machine 1, and all 6 of its tags went in. The cold-room printer was built from a copy of the scanning station's disk and is machine 7, like the scanner, which numbered a line every millisecond from 22:00 to 06:00: 28,800,000 lines. All 9 cold-room tags were refused.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Every number Ingeborg's machines make has three parts. The time: milliseconds since her epoch, the fixed moment every machine counts from, by that machine's clock. The machine number. And the count, which starts at 0 in each millisecond and goes up by one for each extra number made in it. Two numbers can only match if all three parts match. So look at your refused tag at 22:17:41.302 and the row it clashed with. When was that row loaded, and by which machine? Then look at what the cold-room printer was built from, and ask where each machine gets its machine number. Last, ask what Ingeborg means by the machine's own clock. Which time does it read, and can it ever read a millisecond twice?

replies.author: u/night_book_philomena
replies.text: Ingeborg opened the cold-room printer's settings. Machine number: 7. Nobody typed it in. It came with the disk.

comments.author: u/stepped_clock_anatoly
comments.text: Which clock, though? Most machines keep time with NTP, a service that checks the clock against time servers over the network and corrects it. Usually it nudges a clock a little faster or slower until it agrees, but when a clock is far enough out, NTP can step it, and a step can go backwards. Our homegrown generator handed out a run of numbers twice, the night NTP stepped one of our servers back a fraction of a second. Twitter's Snowflake README covers it: if the clock goes backwards, Snowflake refuses to make numbers until its clock is past the last time it used. And if Ingeborg's machines read the wall clock in local time, they have a much bigger step coming. The clocks go back at 02:00 on Sunday.

replies.author: u/night_book_philomena
replies.text: Ingeborg says they read the wall clock, local time, the same time as the night book. The scanner runs straight through 02:00 on Sunday.

comments.author: u/hyphen_count_ximena
comments.text: Or drop the clock and the machine numbers altogether. A UUID is a 128-bit ID that any machine can make on its own. Version 4 is 122 random bits, and written out it's 36 characters: 32 hexadecimal digits and 4 hyphens. That's a mouthful on a tag, and random keys land all over the database's index instead of next to the last one. We moved our database keys to version 7, which starts with 48 bits of Unix time in milliseconds, so new keys sort roughly by time and land together.

comments.author: u/two_counters_orrin
comments.text: We went the other way: back to counters, but two of them, like Flickr's ticket servers. One hands out odd numbers and the other even ones, and you go round robin between them, so if one dies the other carries on. It's still a trip per number, though, and a counter tells the world your volume. Anyone who sees two of your tags a week apart can subtract and know how many records the city made in between.

comments.author: u/short_code_zenobia
comments.text: Side note, since it's how I found this thread: our council wants a short code for every line in its old registers, so families can share a link to an ancestor, like a URL shortener's. Base62 uses 0 to 9, a to z and A to Z, so each character is one of 62. Six characters give 56,800,235,584 codes. One warning from experience: if you pick codes at random, a repeat turns up long before you run out. With six characters it's more likely than not by about 280,600 codes.

replies.author: u/night_book_philomena
replies.text: That's ours too. Ingeborg says six characters is plenty for a billion things. The family-history page opens in March.

reply.prompt: The clocks go back an hour at 02:00 on Sunday, and the scanner runs straight through it. What should Ingeborg change before tonight's shift? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Go back to the town hall counter for every number. One counter can never hand out the same number twice, and no clock change can ever touch it.
options.verdict: No repeats, and one place to fail
options.part2: Ingeborg pointed all three machines back at the town hall counter on Friday afternoon. Nothing has been refused since, and Sunday's clock change passed without a ripple. But every number is a 25 ms trip again, one at a time, so the scanner numbers 40 lines a second: 1,152,000 a night instead of 28,800,000, so the old registers will take 25 times as long to load. Then on Wednesday 11 November the town hall's database went down at 23:20 for two hours. The scanner stopped, and neither printer made a tag. The night shift wrote numbers on cards by hand, as in July, and I copied them into the Casebook in the morning.
options.senior: One counter is simple, ordered and never repeats, but every number costs a trip to one place: its speed is one round trip at a time, and when it's down, nothing gets a number. A counter also tells anyone holding two numbers how many records came in between. Flickr splits the work across two counters, odd and even, so one can fail; Twitter left counters behind so each machine could make numbers alone.

options.text: Hand out machine numbers from one list at startup, so the cold-room printer gets 8. Count in UTC, wait out backward steps, alert on refusals.
options.part2: Ingeborg added a table of machine numbers to the Casebook: each machine claims a free number when it starts, and the table's unique key refuses a second claim. The desk printer kept 1, the scanner 7, and the cold-room printer got 8. On Saturday afternoon she switched all three to count in UTC, with a guard: each machine remembers the last millisecond it used and waits if its clock reads earlier. In summer UTC is an hour behind our clocks, so the switch was itself an hour's step back. The guard would have held any machine that had made a number in the last hour, but the scanner had stopped at 06:00, the cold-room printer was idle and the desk printer's last tag was two hours old, so nothing waited. At 02:00 on Sunday the clocks went back, and the numbers didn't notice. On Monday 9 November at 04:12, NTP stepped the scanner's clock back 250 ms. The guard held it for 249 ms, until its clock read the last millisecond it had used, and the next line got count 1 in that millisecond. Nothing was refused. The alert never fired, and Ingeborg read about the step in the guard's log the next morning.
options.senior: Each part of a Snowflake-style number has to be unique by construction. Machine numbers come from one place, once, at startup, so a copied disk can't bring a twin. Time comes from UTC, which has no daylight saving, and a guard covers the steps NTP can still make: remember the last millisecond used and never go below it. Twitter's README says the same and adds: run NTP in a mode that won't move the clock backwards. The alert turns the next surprise into a message instead of a pile of bad tags.

options.text: Give the cold-room printer its own machine number, 8, today. That's the only clash in the log, so the clocks and the scanner can stay as they are now.
options.part2: Ingeborg gave the cold-room printer machine number 8 on Friday afternoon, and that night all its tags went in. Then at 02:00 on Sunday the clocks went back an hour. Every machine's count went back with them, and the scanner, still running, made again, millisecond by millisecond, every number it had made between 01:00 and 02:00. The Casebook refused 3,600,000 lines. Ingeborg found them at 07:00 in the scanner's error log, one line each, and spent Sunday loading them again with new numbers.
options.senior: A machine number fixes one way to repeat a number: two machines sharing one. A clock that reads a millisecond twice is the other, and a wall clock in local time does it every October for a whole hour. Count in UTC, which never steps for daylight saving, and guard against the smaller steps NTP can make. And find out where every machine's number comes from, so the next copied disk can't bring a twin.

options.text: Drop the clocks and machine numbers and switch every machine to random UUID v4s. With 122 random bits, a repeat is far too unlikely to plan for.
options.part2: Ingeborg switched every machine to UUID v4 on Saturday. No number has been refused since, and Sunday's clock change did nothing at all. But each tag now carries 36 characters instead of 18 digits, in a smaller font, and the Casebook stores 16 bytes per number instead of 8. Sorting the night book by number no longer puts it in time order: Saturday night's tags come out in random order, and so do the scanner's lines. Ingeborg is now adding a time column to every table so that anyone can find last night again.
options.senior: Random UUIDs need no coordination at all: no machine numbers, no clock, and with 122 random bits a repeat among a billion is about a 1 in 10^19 chance. You pay in size, 16 bytes or 36 characters, and in order: they don't sort by time, and new keys land all over the index. UUID v7 keeps the independence, puts 48 bits of Unix milliseconds first so keys sort roughly by time, and keeps 74 random bits.

sim.title: Number the night at the Marrowgate mortuary
sim.lede: You're Ingeborg, replaying Thursday night, 22 October, from 22:00. The scanning station numbers one line of the old registers every millisecond until 06:00 by the wall clock. The desk printer and the cold-room printer make the night's tags at the times in Philomena's log, and you can add an arrival at either. Pick how numbers are made: Snowflake-style (41 bits of milliseconds since 1 January 2026, a 10-bit machine number and a 12-bit count), the town hall counter (one 25 ms trip per number, one trip at a time), two ticket servers at the town hall (A odd, B even, round robin), UUID v4 or UUID v7. For Snowflake, pick the cold-room printer's machine number, whether machines count from the wall clock in local time or in UTC, and the clock guard, which waits while a machine's clock reads earlier than the last millisecond it used. Within one millisecond the scanner goes first. The Casebook refuses any number it already holds, and the sim counts those refusals as duplicates. UUIDs are drawn from the sim's seeded random numbers; the sim doesn't store millions of them and counts no repeats. The clock runs a minute a second, and changing a setting replays the night. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: skip to the end of the night. 9 duplicates, all from the cold-room printer, which shares machine 7 with the scanner. Give it its own number, 8, which replays the night from 22:00. Skip four hours to 02:00, press The clocks go back an hour, and skip one more hour: no tag is refused, but 3,600,000 lines are, as the scanner relives 01:00 to 02:00. Switch the machines to UTC, which replays the night, and do the same: none. Then step the scanner's clock back 250 ms with NTP and let it run a few seconds: 250 duplicates. Turn the guard on, which replays again, skip an hour and step it back again: the scanner waits 249 ms instead, and nothing is refused. Then try the town hall counter: 40 lines a second, and nothing at all while it's down. Two ticket servers carry on with one down. UUID v4 needs no machine numbers or clock, but look at the sort stat. Last, change how many codes you need and read the base62 length.

explain.oneLine: Nobody in the old registers took those numbers. The cold-room printer was a disk copy of the scanner, so both were machine 7, and the scanner had used every millisecond's number with count 0 before the printer did. And the clocks going back on Sunday would have made the scanner repeat a whole hour.

steps.title: Three parts, and each one has to be unique.
steps.text: A Snowflake-style number is three numbers packed into one 64-bit integer: 41 bits of milliseconds since an epoch, a 10-bit machine number and a 12-bit count. Twitter's 2010 README gives the arithmetic: 41 bits of milliseconds give 69 years, 10 bits give up to 1024 machines, and the count rolls over every 4096 per machine. So one machine can make 4,096 numbers a millisecond, 4,096,000 a second, and 41 + 10 + 12 = 63 bits, so the number stays positive in a signed 64-bit integer. Nobody is asked when a number is made: uniqueness comes from the parts. So there are only two ways to repeat one. Two running machines share a machine number, or one machine's clock reads a millisecond it has already read. Ingeborg's cold-room printer was a disk copy of the scanner, so both were machine 7. The scanner makes a number every millisecond with count 0, so every tag the printer made, also count 0, landed on a number the scanner had made in the same millisecond: 9 of 9.

steps.title: Clocks that go backwards.
steps.text: A wall clock in local time reads an hour twice every October. At 02:00 on Sunday the clocks go back, and the scanner would make again, millisecond by millisecond, the 3,600,000 numbers it made between 01:00 and 02:00. NTP can do the same in smaller steps: when a clock is far enough out, NTP may step it back. RFC 9562, the UUID standard, says that if it is possible for the system clock to move backward due to either manual adjustment or corrections from a time synchronization protocol, implementations need to determine how to handle such cases. There are three defences. Count in UTC, or Unix time, which never steps for daylight saving. Ask NTP to slew rather than step where you can. And keep the last millisecond used: if the clock reads earlier, wait until it catches up, or refuse, as Twitter's code does. In the sim, a 250 ms step makes 250 duplicates without that guard. With it, the scanner waits 249 ms and then uses count 1 in the millisecond it last used.

steps.title: Counters: one place hands out every number.
steps.text: Auto-increment is the simplest unique ID: one database adds one to a counter for each new row. The numbers are small, ordered and never repeat. But one place hands out every number. Its speed is a trip to it, and when it's down, nothing gets a number: Philomena's printer on 3 July, and a scanner that waits for each 25 ms trip numbers 40 lines a second instead of 1,000. Counters don't merge, either: split a table across two databases, each with its own counter, and both hand out 1, 2, 3. And they leak. Anyone who sees two numbers can subtract and know how many rows were made in between, and can guess the next one. Flickr kept counters but runs two ticket servers, one handing out odd numbers and the other even ones, with requests going round robin between them, so either can die and the other carries on. They drift apart, so the numbers are only roughly in order.

steps.title: UUIDs: no coordination at all.
steps.text: A UUID is 128 bits that any machine can make on its own; RFC 9562 says no centralized authority is required to administer them. Version 4 is 122 random bits, plus 6 bits that mark the version and variant. Among a billion of them, the chance that any two match is about 1 in 10^19: n squared over 2 to the 123rd. The cost is size and order: 16 bytes instead of 8, 36 characters as text, and no time order at all. Random keys land at random places in an index, and the RFC warns that the effects on B-trees can be dramatic. Version 7 keeps the independence and brings back most of the order. Its first 48 bits are Unix time in milliseconds, then come the version and variant bits and 74 random bits, so new keys sort roughly by time and land next to each other. Its timestamp lasts until the year 10889. It still reads a clock: after a step back, new v7s sort before ones made just earlier, though their random bits keep them from repeating.

steps.title: Choosing, and short codes.
steps.text: Ask four questions. Must IDs sort by time? Auto-increment does. UUID v7 and Snowflake do roughly: exactly to the millisecond within one machine, but machines' clocks differ a little. UUID v4 not at all. How big may they be? 8 bytes for a counter or a Snowflake number, 16 for a UUID. Who has to agree? A counter needs one place for every number; Snowflake needs unique machine numbers once, at startup, and clocks that never step back; UUIDs need nobody. And what do they tell strangers? Counters tell volume and can be guessed. Snowflake numbers tell when, and on which machine. None of them is a password, so check access on every lookup. Short codes are the same arithmetic in another alphabet. Base62 has 62 symbols, so L characters give 62^L codes: 62^5 = 916,132,832 is short of a billion, and 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 is enough. A billion codes need 6 characters and a trillion need 7. Codes made from a unique number never clash. Codes picked at random clash long before they run out: with 6 characters, a repeat is more likely than not by about 280,600 codes, so check each new one against those already issued. This season's 3 AM Interview, a URL shortener, starts here.

notes.text: Clocks go back at 02:00 on 25 October. UTC doesn't, so nothing repeats.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the night after. Each machine claims its machine number from one table when it starts, and the table refuses a second claim, so a copied disk can't bring a twin: the cold-room printer is now machine 8. All three machines count milliseconds in UTC, which doesn't change when the clocks go back, and each one waits if its clock ever reads earlier than the last millisecond it used. The Casebook keeps its unique key, and any refusal raises an alert.

fix.title: The fix: machine numbers from one place, UTC, a guard, and an alert
fix.text: Add a table of machine numbers to the Casebook: each machine claims a free number at startup, and the table's unique key refuses a second claim, so a machine built from a copied disk has to claim its own. Give the cold-room printer 8. Count milliseconds in UTC rather than the wall clock, so 02:00 on Sunday is just another hour. Make the switch while the machines are idle, because in summer UTC is an hour behind the wall clock and the switch is itself a step back. Keep the last millisecond each machine used, and if its clock ever reads earlier, wait until it catches up: a 250 ms NTP step costs the scanner 249 ms. Ask NTP to slew rather than step where the machines allow it. And raise an alert on any refusal from the Casebook, because a unique key that refuses quietly is evidence nobody reads.

limits: Handing out machine numbers at startup moves the coordination, it doesn't remove it. The table must be reachable when a machine starts, and a machine restored from a disk copy must claim again rather than trust the number it carries. Twitter's 2010 post says its worker numbers are chosen at startup through ZooKeeper, for the same reason.

The guard waits as long as the step. That's 249 ms for a 250 ms NTP step, but a whole hour for a machine still counting local time when the clocks go back. Switching a busy machine from local time to UTC in summer is a one-hour step back too, so switch while it's idle or accept that it waits. And even with the guard, Snowflake numbers are only roughly in time order across machines. Each machine's clock is a little off, so a number made on one machine can sort before one made a few milliseconds earlier on another. Twitter promised 1 second and aimed for tens of milliseconds.

The numbers aren't secret. Each one carries the millisecond it was made and the machine that made it, so anyone holding a tag can read when it was printed, and nearby numbers can be tried. Never let knowing a number be enough to open a record; check access on every lookup. Nor do they last forever: forty-one bits from 1 January 2026 run out in September 2095. And these numbers are too big for JavaScript to hold exactly: above 2^53, 9,007,199,254,740,992, not every whole number fits, and at the size of these tags only multiples of 16 do, so a number with a count of 1 comes back as its neighbour. Send them to web pages as strings. Even the ones it holds exactly print wrong: 106886353467215872 shows as 106886353467215870.

explain.seniorTake: An ID scheme is a promise that no two things ever share a number, and every scheme pays for it somewhere. A counter pays with a trip to one place for every number, and tells strangers your volume. A random UUID pays with size and order. A Snowflake-style number pays with two promises of your own: no two running machines share a machine number, and no machine's clock reads a millisecond twice. Make both mechanical. Hand out machine numbers from one table at startup, count in UTC, guard against steps back, and alert on the first duplicate-key error, because the database's unique key is the last line of defence and its refusals are the only evidence. Then pick by what the IDs must do: sort by time, fit in 8 bytes, survive a dead server, or reveal nothing. And never let an ID stand in for an access check.

realWorld.title: Twitter, June 2010: an uncoordinated approach
realWorld.text: Twitter's engineering blog announced Snowflake on Tuesday 1 June 2010, as it moved data from MySQL to Cassandra and to sharded MySQL. The post's requirements: "We needed something that could generate tens of thousands of ids per second in a highly available manner. This naturally led us to choose an uncoordinated approach." The IDs had to be roughly sortable, "meaning that if tweets A and B are posted around the same time, they should have ids in close proximity to one another", and "these numbers have to fit into 64 bits." It lists what Twitter turned down: "MySQL-based ticket servers (like flickr uses), but those didn't give us the ordering guarantees we needed without building some sort of re-syncing routine"; UUIDs, because "all the schemes we could find required 128 bits"; and Zookeeper sequential nodes, where Twitter "feared that the coordinated approach would lower our availability for no real payoff." It settled on "a composition of: timestamp, worker number and sequence number. Sequence numbers are per-thread and worker numbers are chosen at startup via zookeeper (though that's overridable via a config file)." A footnote says the tweets would be k-sorted, with k below 1 second. The post called the code alpha-quality software that Twitter wasn't yet running in production.

realWorld.title: The Snowflake README: the layout, and the clock
realWorld.text: The README on the project's snowflake-2010 tag opens: "Snowflake is a network service for generating unique ID numbers at high scale with some simple guarantees." It asks for a "minimum 10k ids per second per process", says that "machines generating ids should not have to coordinate with each other", and that "we need to keep our ids under 64bits." The id is composed of: "time - 41 bits (millisecond precision w/ a custom epoch gives us 69 years)", "configured machine id - 10 bits - gives us up to 1024 machines" and "sequence number - 12 bits - rolls over every 4096 per machine (with protection to avoid rollover in the same ms)". On clocks: "You should use NTP to keep your system clock accurate." Snowflake protects from clocks that run backwards: "If your clock is running fast and NTP tells it to repeat a few milliseconds, snowflake will refuse to generate ids until a time that is after the last time we generated an id. Even better, run in a mode where ntp won't move the clock backwards." The arithmetic checks: 2^41 milliseconds is about 69.7 years.

realWorld.title: Inside IdWorker: refuse, or wait for the next millisecond
realWorld.text: The Scala code on the same tag shows the guard. Its custom epoch, twepoch, is 1288834974657, which is 01:42:54.657 UTC on 4 November 2010, so its 41 bits last until July 2080. The 10 machine bits are split into a 5-bit datacenter ID and a 5-bit worker ID. When the timestamp is earlier than the last one used, the code logs an error and throws an InvalidSystemClock exception whose message begins "Clock moved backwards." When it's the same millisecond, the sequence goes up by one, kept within 12 bits; if that wraps to 0, the code waits for the next millisecond. Otherwise the sequence starts again at 0. Ingeborg's guard in this case waits instead of refusing; both keep a machine from reusing a millisecond.

realWorld.title: Flickr's ticket servers: odd and even
realWorld.text: Flickr's engineering blog described its ticket servers on 8 February 2010. "Ticket servers give us globally (Flickr-wide) unique integers to serve as primary keys in our distributed setup." They're needed because Flickr shards its data across many databases, and MySQL can't guarantee uniqueness across physical and logical databases. Flickr didn't use GUIDs, "Mostly because GUIDs are big, and they index badly in MySQL", and it liked the sequentiality, which makes reporting and debugging more straightforward. Each ticket server is a dedicated MySQL database server with tables like Tickets64, which holds a single row, and a new 64-bit ID is one REPLACE INTO on that table followed by SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID(). To avoid a single point of failure, Flickr runs two: one with auto-increment-increment = 2 and auto-increment-offset = 1, the other with offset 2, dividing the ID space into odds and evens, and it goes round robin between them to load balance and deal with down time. The post admits the sides drift: a few hundred thousand more odd number objects than even ones at the time, "but this hurts no one." It says the scheme had been in production since Friday the 13th, January 2006.

realWorld.title: RFC 9562: UUIDs, version 4 and version 7
realWorld.text: RFC 9562, published in May 2024, replaces RFC 4122 as the UUID standard. It says no centralized authority is required to administer UUIDs, and that auto-increment schemes often used by databases do not work well across a network, because "the effort required to coordinate sequential numeric identifiers across a network can easily become a burden." UUID v4 has 122 random bits. It warns that UUID versions that are not time ordered, such as UUIDv4, have poor database-index locality: new values "require inserts to be performed at random locations", and the effects on B-trees "can be dramatic". UUID v7 starts with the number of milliseconds since midnight 1 January 1970 UTC in 48 bits, "valid until the year 10889 AD", and fills the rest with random bits and an optional counter. The RFC says time-ordered values benefit from greater database-index locality, by one order of magnitude or more in the real world. It asks implementations to handle clocks that move backward, to store UUIDs as 128-bit binary rather than text (text takes 288 bits), and it says UUIDs "MUST NOT be used as security capabilities (identifiers whose mere possession grants access)."

realWorld.title: X today: send big IDs as strings
realWorld.text: X's developer documentation says X IDs are 64-bit unsigned integers generated using Snowflake, each encoding a timestamp, a worker number and a sequence number, so IDs are roughly time-ordered. It tells developers: "Always use string IDs in your code. Some programming languages (like JavaScript) can't accurately represent 64-bit integers." In JavaScript, it says, integers are limited to 53 bits. API v2 returns IDs as strings by default, and v1.1 returns both id and id_str, with the advice to always use id_str.

realWorld.title: OWASP: a hard-to-guess ID is not access control
realWorld.text: OWASP's cheat sheet on Insecure Direct Object Reference, IDOR, says the vulnerability occurs due to missing access control checks, and its example is changing a number in a URL from one user's ID to the next. It says complex identifiers like GUIDs can make it practically impossible to guess valid values, but that even with complex identifiers, access control checks are essential. Its advice: implement access control checks for each object, and "use complex identifiers as a defense-in-depth measure, but remember that access control is crucial even with these identifiers."

asked: Design a unique ID generator for a distributed system.
UUID, Snowflake or auto-increment: which would you use, and when?
How many characters do you need for a short URL code?
interview.answer: Start with the requirements: how many IDs a second, whether they must sort by time, how big they may be, whether they appear in URLs, and what happens if the generator is unreachable. Then the options. An auto-increment column in one database is simple, compact and ordered, but every ID is a trip to one place, it's a single point of failure, it leaks volume, and separate counters clash when shards are merged. Ticket servers, like Flickr's odd and even pair, keep counters but survive one failure. UUID v4 needs no coordination at all, at 16 bytes and with random index inserts; UUID v7 puts a 48-bit millisecond timestamp first, so keys sort roughly by time. A Snowflake-style 64-bit ID packs 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, a 10-bit machine number and a 12-bit sequence: 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine, about 69 years, no coordination per ID. Its two risks are two machines with the same machine number and a clock that steps back, so hand out machine numbers at startup from one place, count in UTC, run NTP so it slews, and refuse or wait when the clock reads earlier than the last timestamp. For short codes, do the arithmetic: base62 gives 62^L codes, 62^6 = 56,800,235,584, so 6 characters cover a billion and 7 cover 3.5 trillion. Encode a unique ID or counter rather than picking at random, or check every random code, because random codes collide after about the square root of the space.

terms.def: A building where the dead are kept until a funeral or an inquiry. This case's is the city mortuary on Marrowgate.
The paper book the mortuary's night shift keeps: one line per arrival, with its tag number. Philomena keeps it.
In the night book, anyone brought in to the mortuary. Each arrival gets a line in the book and a tag.
The paper label printed for each arrival, carrying its number. The same number is the arrival's key in the Casebook.
The mortuary's records database. Its number column has a unique key, so it refuses any number it already holds.
The counter in the town hall's database that gave out every number until July: one 25 ms trip per number.
Machine 7, in the mortuary basement. From 22:00 to 06:00 it loads lines of the city's old registers into the Casebook, one line a millisecond, each with its own number.
The city's paper books of births, deaths and burials going back more than a century, loaded into the Casebook line by line.
The mortuary's refrigerated room. The night shift's new tag printer stands at its door.
The person who looks after a records office's computers and databases. Here, Ingeborg.
An exact copy of one machine's disk, used to set up another. Everything on it comes too, including settings such as a machine number.
Making IDs that are never used twice, often on many machines at once, and ideally without them having to ask each other.
A database constraint that refuses a second row with the same value in a column. The Casebook's refuses repeated numbers.
A database column that fills itself with the last number plus one for each new row. Simple and ordered, but one database hands out every number.
One of several databases that each hold part of a table's rows. Splitting the rows up this way is called sharding.
Machines checking with each other, or with one shared place, before acting. It costs a trip each time, and stops when that place is down.
Twitter's 2010 ID service: 64-bit numbers made from a timestamp, a machine number and a sequence number, with no coordination per ID.
Any 64-bit ID built like Snowflake's: milliseconds since an epoch, a machine number and a count. Ingeborg's is one.
A whole number stored in 64 bits, 8 bytes. A signed one goes up to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807, which is 19 digits.
The fixed moment a clock-based ID counts from. Ingeborg's is midnight on 1 January 2026; Twitter's code uses one in November 2010.
The part of a Snowflake-style ID that says which machine made it. Ten bits give 1,024 of them, and every running machine needs its own. Twitter calls it the worker number.
The part of a Snowflake-style ID that numbers what one machine makes within one millisecond: 0, then 1, 2 and so on up to 4,095. Twitter calls it the sequence number.
The time a machine shows people: local time, which jumps for daylight saving.
Moving clocks an hour ahead for summer. When it ends, as at 02:00 on 25 October, local time goes back an hour and 01:00 to 02:00 happens twice.
Time counted in seconds or milliseconds since midnight on 1 January 1970 UTC. It ignores time zones and daylight saving.
Network Time Protocol: the service that keeps a machine's clock in step with time servers over the network.
Two ways to correct a clock. A step jumps it to the right time at once, perhaps backwards; a slew runs it slightly fast or slow until it agrees.
Code that keeps the last millisecond an ID generator used and, if the clock reads earlier, waits or refuses until it catches up.
The fix's table in the Casebook: a machine claims a free machine number when it starts, and the unique key refuses a second claim on the same one.
A number the Casebook refuses because it already holds it. The sim counts them.
Universally unique identifier: a 128-bit ID any machine can make on its own, written as 32 hexadecimal digits in five groups with hyphens, 36 characters.
Globally unique identifier: another name for a UUID. Flickr's post and OWASP's cheat sheet use it.
A UUID made of 122 random bits plus 6 fixed bits for the version and variant. No clock, no machine number, no order.
A UUID that starts with 48 bits of Unix time in milliseconds, then the version and variant bits and 74 random bits. New ones sort roughly by time: to the millisecond within a machine.
Writing numbers in base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and a to f. Each digit is 4 bits, so 128 bits is 32 digits.
Whether new keys land near each other in a database index. Time-ordered keys go in at one end; random keys land anywhere in it.
The sorted tree most databases use for indexes, stored in fixed-size pages. RFC 9562 warns that random inserts can slow it dramatically.
In order to within a bound. Twitter calls it k-sorted: an ID made up to k earlier may sort after a later one. Twitter aimed for k under 1 second.
A database whose only job is handing out unique numbers from a counter. Flickr runs two, one for odd numbers and one for even ones.
A widely used open-source SQL database. Twitter stored most of its data in it in 2010; Flickr's ticket servers are MySQL databases.
MySQL statements. REPLACE INTO writes a row, replacing any row with the same unique key; LAST_INSERT_ID() returns the auto-increment number just used.
A database that spreads data across many machines. Twitter was moving data to it in 2010, and it has no built-in sequential IDs.
A service that helps machines agree on small shared facts, such as which worker number each one has. Twitter's Snowflake picked worker numbers through it.
The programming language Twitter wrote Snowflake in.
The social network that built Snowflake in 2010, now called X. X's developer docs describe the IDs it uses today.
A photo-sharing site. Its engineers described their ticket servers on their blog in 2010.
The 2024 standard that defines UUIDs, including versions 4 and 7. It replaces RFC 4122.
Writing numbers with 62 symbols: 0 to 9, a to z and A to Z. L characters give 62 to the power L different codes.
The few characters at the end of a short link, as from a URL shortener, that stand for a longer address or a record.
Picking at random from N values, a repeat becomes likely after about the square root of N picks, long before N runs out. Named after shared birthdays in a room.
How many things a business makes, such as orders a day. Sequential IDs shown to customers reveal it to anyone who compares two.
Insecure Direct Object Reference: a page or API returns an object for any ID it's given, without checking the caller may see it.
The code that checks, on every request, whether this caller may see or change this particular record.
Several protections stacked, so one failing isn't enough for an attacker. OWASP counts hard-to-guess IDs as one layer, never the only one.
The programming language of web pages. Its ordinary numbers hold whole numbers exactly only up to 2^53, 9,007,199,254,740,992.

atWork: Picture a team that showed order numbers like #104233 on receipts, straight from an auto-increment column. A rival placed an order every Monday, subtracted, and knew their weekly sales; another team's homegrown time-based generator handed out duplicate IDs the night NTP stepped a server's clock back, and nobody noticed until a payment was matched to the wrong order. Check your own systems for both. List every ID that leaves the building: order, invoice and ticket numbers, user IDs in URLs. For each, find how it's made: a database auto-increment, a sequence several services share, UUID v4, UUID v7, or a homegrown generator. For sequential public IDs, place two test orders a day apart and subtract; if the difference tells you yesterday's sales, it tells a competitor too. The fix is an opaque public ID, with the counter kept internal, and an access check on every lookup by ID, as OWASP's IDOR cheat sheet says. For a homegrown generator, read the code: where does the machine number come from, and what stops two machines sharing one after a disk copy or an autoscaling launch? Which clock does it read, local time or UTC, and what does it do when that clock reads earlier than its last ID? Ask how NTP is set up on those hosts. The fixes are the ones in this case: machine numbers handed out at startup, UTC, a guard that waits or refuses, and an alert on any duplicate-key error.

recall.prompt: A food delivery start-up gives every order an auto-increment number from its single PostgreSQL database and prints it on the receipt. A rival orders lunch from it every Monday and now knows the start-up's weekly order count. Next month the team will split orders across four databases, each with its own auto-increment column. What goes wrong, and what would you use instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Sequential numbers leak volume: the difference between two receipts is the orders in between, and the next number can be guessed
Four separate counters each start from 1, so the databases hand out the same numbers and orders clash
Make IDs without a shared counter: Snowflake-style with a unique machine number per server, UUID v7, or counters with different offsets
Keep the internal key private: show customers an ID that reveals nothing, and check access on every lookup

recall.model: The receipts leak volume. The numbers go up by one per order, so subtracting last Monday's from this Monday's gives a week of orders, and anyone can guess the next order's number. Splitting across four databases makes it worse: four auto-increment columns each start from 1, so every number is handed out four times, and orders clash as soon as anything joins or merges them. Use IDs no shared counter hands out: Snowflake-style 64-bit numbers with a machine number unique to each server, claimed at startup, and a UTC clock with a guard; or UUID v7 if 16 bytes is fine. If they must stay counters, give each database its own offset, the way Flickr's two ticket servers split odd and even. Either way, don't print an internal key on receipts: show an opaque public ID, and check on every lookup that the caller may see that order.

recall.prompt: In Twitter's Snowflake layout the sequence number is 12 bits. How many IDs can one machine make in one millisecond before it has to wait for the next?
recall.why: 2^12 = 4,096. The README says the sequence number rolls over every 4096 per machine, with protection to avoid rollover in the same millisecond, so the code waits for the next one. That's 4,096,000 a second per machine. 1,024 is the number of machines 10 bits allow, and 4,194,304 is 2^22, the numbers per millisecond across all 1,024 machines.

recall.prompt: A URL shortener will hand out up to 1,000,000,000 codes in base62 (0 to 9, a to z, A to Z). What's the shortest code length that gives each one a different code?
recall.why: 62^5 = 916,132,832, which is short of a billion; 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 is enough. That's only true if codes come from a unique number, such as a counter or an ID written in base62. Pick 6-character codes at random and a repeat is more likely than not by about 280,600 codes, so random codes must be checked against those already issued.

recall.prompt: NTP steps the clock of a Snowflake-style generator back 250 ms while it's making one ID a millisecond. It has no clock guard. What happens?
options: It repeats the IDs of the last 250 ms
Nothing: the machine number keeps every one of its IDs unique
It stops until someone restarts it
Its IDs sort before older ones from then on, but none is a repeat
recall.why: The time part is the only part that changes from one millisecond to the next. When the clock reads a millisecond again, the generator starts the count at 0 again, and timestamp, machine number and count all match an ID it already made: 250 repeats. Twitter's code refuses to make IDs while the clock reads earlier than the last one used; a guard that waits does the same job.

recall.prompt: Why does RFC 9562 say UUID v4 keys can hurt a database index, and what does UUID v7 change?
options: v4 is 16 bytes and v7 is 8, so v7 fits twice as many keys in each index page
v4 repeats about once in a billion IDs, and v7's timestamp makes repeats impossible
v4 needs a central server to hand values out, and v7 can be made on each machine
v4 lands at random in the index; v7 starts with time, so new keys land together
recall.why: Both versions are 128 bits and need no coordination. The RFC says versions that aren't time ordered, such as v4, have poor database-index locality: new values need inserts at random locations, and the effects on B-trees can be dramatic. v7 puts 48 bits of Unix milliseconds first, so values made in succession sit next to each other in the index.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 7 months later. The council's family-history page opened in March. Anyone can look up a line in the old registers and make a share link ending in a 6-character base62 code, which Ingeborg's script picks at random. "Fifty-six billion codes," she said. "We'll never run out." Her table keeps one record per code, and the newest wins. The page has made 312,450 links so far. On Tuesday a man opened the link his cousin sent him in April for their great-grandmother's burial in 1903, and the page showed a stranger's line instead: a man buried in 1917. His cousin says the link worked when she made it.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What's going on, and what should Ingeborg change?

keyIdeas.idea: Random codes repeat long before the space runs out (the birthday problem): with 6 base62 characters a repeat is more likely than not by about 280,600 codes, so the cousin's code was given out again
Stop new clashes: a unique key that refuses instead of replacing, picking again on a clash, or codes made from a unique number such as a counter or Snowflake ID in base62
Find the codes given out twice and restore the older links; a longer code makes clashes rarer but doesn't remove them

coldCase.model: Ingeborg's codes are picked at random, and random picks repeat long before the space runs out: the birthday problem. With 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 possible codes, a repeat becomes more likely than not by about 280,600 codes, and the page has made 312,450. The cousin's code was drawn again for someone else's link, and because the table keeps one record per code and the newest wins, her link now opens the stranger's line. Fix new codes first: give the code column a unique key that refuses rather than replaces, and pick again on a clash, or make codes from a unique number, such as a counter or a Snowflake-style ID written in base62, which never clash. Then find the codes that were given out twice and restore the older links. Seven characters would make clashes rarer, not impossible.
